todayTheme: Checking whether an agent behaved correctly is its own fragile measurement problem: static test suites miss multi-turn policy violations, published safety-guard accuracy can swing on cosmetic benchmark rewording, and the standard 'retrieval failure' diagnosis in RAG evals hides which bottleneck actually needs fixing

candidates.title: PROBE: Learning to Audit Policy Compliance in Tool-Using LLM Agents
candidates.venue: NeurIPS 2026 (main conference, accepted; per arXiv Comments field '27 pages, NeurIPS 2026')
candidates.citationVelocity: not retrieved (Semantic Scholar persistent 429 across entire run)
candidates.institution: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI), Abu Dhabi, UAE (all 4 authors: Kshitij Mishra, Abhijith Sharma, Nils Lukas, Salem Lahlou)
communitySignals: not confirmed on partial HF Daily Papers 10-16 recovery
no Papers with Code entry found
credibilityEvidence: Sec 3: formal two-player partially-observed Markov game definition of policy-compliance auditing, with trace-level verifiers over dialogue+tool calls+outputs+state (not token-level)

Sec 5-6: controlled comparison of GRPO/DPO/GFlowNet optimizers training a 4B auditor (QLoRA, ~47M trainable params) against a frozen 30B target on 50 held-out scenarios; headline metric is suite-level policy coverage (12/20 policies vs 7/20 for zero-shot 30B auditor vs 1/20 for random)

Sec 6.3: human validation of 208 judge-scored instances finds the LLM judge agrees with two human annotators only 39.6% of the time (kappa=0.084) despite near-perfect human-human agreement (kappa=0.985); authors identify GRPO exploiting this judge error and report deterministic re-scoring that removes the affected policy, dropping best coverage from 60% to 55% while keeping the ranking unchanged
Sec 6.4: transfer tests to an unseen Gemma target family (40% vs 55% in-domain coverage) and to tau-bench with a different base model (coverage 2->3 of 10 policies, violations +123%)

Sec 7 Limitations (self-disclosed): only 2 environments and 2 target families tested; auditor rarely drives the target past search (>90% of tool calls), so high-severity booking/mutation-level policies remain largely unreached; 2 of the human annotators are the authors themselves
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Covers method, three-optimizer ablation, human-judge validation with an honestly reported failure mode, deterministic re-scoring, and two independent transfer tests (unseen model family, unseen benchmark); still limited to 2 synthetic tool environments.
reproducibilityEvidence: Extensive algorithmic, reward, and prompt detail given in the main text and appendices (reward formula, optimizer hyperparameters, scenario generation), but no public code/weights repository link found in the abstract, HTML body, or comments field
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: Article only states claims validated under the held-out/transfer protocol and explicitly carries over the authors' own judge-reliability caveat rather than treating the headline coverage numbers as unqualified.
candidates.primaryLimitation: The frozen target agent rarely reaches booking/cancellation/modification tool states (>90% of calls are search-only), so the hardest, highest-severity policies remain structurally under-tested regardless of auditor quality.
candidates.presentationReason: Formal game definition, metric definitions, ablation structure, and a dedicated Limitations/Scope section are all explicit and easy to follow.
candidates.reason: Only candidate today that formalizes and solves a genuinely new evaluation axis (multi-turn behavioral policy-compliance auditing) with a NeurIPS-accepted, ablated, human-validated, and transfer-tested study; anchors today's 'is the audit itself trustworthy' theme with the most complete evidence of the three selected papers.

candidates.title: Shortcut Sensitivity in Agent-Safety Evaluations
candidates.venue: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 workshops TAE ('Can We Trust AI Evaluation?') and AIWILD ('Agents in the Wild: Safety, Security, and Beyond') -- workshop-level acceptance, not the main conference
candidates.citationVelocity: not retrieved (Semantic Scholar persistent 429 across entire run)
candidates.institution: Kontext (both authors, Hasan Demirkiran and Jens Ernstberger, are co-founders of Kontext, an AI-agent-security startup that raised a $4M seed round led by 42CAP in Sept 2026, per LinkedIn/press coverage found via web search; this is a disclosed conflict of interest, not stated in the paper itself)
communitySignals: not confirmed on partial HF Daily Papers 10-16 recovery
aggregate code/results package public on GitHub (hasandemirkiran/shortcut-sensitivity-agent-safety-evaluations), explicitly stripped of raw benchmark text/arguments/provider responses
credibilityEvidence: Sec 3-5: three-level shortcut-auditing framework (label predictability / observational guard association / paired decision sensitivity) applied to LinuxArena (576 dedup trajectories), AgentDojo-Traj (1,220 steps), and AgentHarm-Traj (731 steps)

Concrete, reproducible-looking numbers: AgentDojo-Traj exact-tool-lookup F1 falls from .901 (mixed-domain folds) to .495 (domain holdout); AgentHarm-Traj TS-Guard F1 falls from .902 (row weighting) to .719 (equal interaction weighting)

Sec 5.2: a frozen, pre-registered-style 64-step cohort with 960 repeated Claude Haiku 4.5 calls shows marker rewrite lowers blocking by 8.33pp and tool aliasing raises it by 11.46pp, both surviving a formatting-placebo subtraction with 95% bootstrap ranges excluding zero

Sec 5.3 (self-disclosed): the same intervention does NOT reproduce on GPT-5.6 Luna or a quantized Q8 TS-Guard reproduction -- authors explicitly frame the Haiku effect as 'configuration-specific', not a general guard flaw

Sec 8 Limitations (self-disclosed): 64-step cohort is not a probability sample, intervals are exploratory/unadjusted, no blinded human equivalence check on whether the edits actually preserve the safety construct
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: The core causal claim (cue representation materially changes guard decisions) is demonstrated with a real paired intervention and placebo control, but only reproduces for one of three tested guard configurations (Haiku), and the authors themselves label it an instance rather than a prevalence estimate.
reproducibilityEvidence: Aggregate code and results package published on GitHub, but explicitly excludes raw benchmark text, tool arguments, identifiers, and provider responses, so the paired-intervention calls cannot be independently re-run against the original data without separately obtaining the upstream benchmarks
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: The measured F1/accuracy swings are real and placebo-controlled, but the authors' own commercial position (an agent-safety startup whose value proposition benefits from 'published guard benchmarks are unreliable') is a disclosed conflict of interest that readers should weigh alongside the non-reproduction on 2 of 3 guard configurations; this caps confidence at medium rather than high despite solid methodology.
candidates.primaryLimitation: The headline effect (cue edits swinging a guard's measured accuracy) is demonstrated for only one of three tested guard configurations (Claude Haiku 4.5) and does not reproduce on GPT-5.6 Luna or a quantized TS-Guard reproduction; combined with the authors' commercial stake in an agent-safety product, this narrows how far the finding should be generalized.
candidates.presentationReason: Three-level framework, per-dataset methodology, and an explicit Limitations and broader-impact section are all clearly separated and stated.
candidates.reason: Directly tests whether the safety-guard accuracy numbers teams currently publish are measuring real guard behavior or benchmark artifacts, with a genuine placebo-controlled paired intervention; selected as a conditional pass with the author COI and single-configuration reproduction explicitly disclosed in the article, matching this site's established practice of flagging self-interested measurement work rather than excluding it outright.

candidates.title: Beyond Retrieval Failure: Understanding Why LLMs Miss Evidence in Multi-Hop RAG
candidates.venue: DAI 2026 Oral (8th International Conference on Distributed Artificial Intelligence, CCF-C rated, Hong Kong, Nov 30-Dec 1 2026; accepted per arXiv Comments field, confirmed as a real distributed-AI/multi-agent-systems conference via web search)
candidates.citationVelocity: not retrieved (Semantic Scholar persistent 429 across entire run)
candidates.institution: Acknowledgements credit Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory; co-author Wanli Ouyang is a senior Shanghai AI Laboratory-affiliated researcher
communitySignals: not confirmed on partial HF Daily Papers 10-16 recovery
no Papers with Code entry found
credibilityEvidence: Sec 3: ExecutionRAG, a training-free requirement register with 4 explicit item states (pending/active/resolved/retired), holding retriever/corpus/generator fixed relative to a matched baseline (A-RAG) so the only variable is search guidance

Sec 4.3: on 1,000 MuSiQue questions, wrong answers with unretrieved required evidence fall from 382 to 234 (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) and from 383 to 274 (Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B) -- a matched A-RAG-vs-ExecutionRAG comparison, not a cross-paper number

Sec 4.3-4.4: evidence recovery does NOT proportionally reduce total error -- reasoning errors after retrieval rise from 9% to 26% (MiniLM) and abstentions from 7% to 13%, which the authors interpret honestly as a partial observability artifact rather than claiming the generator 'reasons worse'
Sec 4.5: the same directional result replicates across a second embedding backbone (Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B) on all 3 benchmarks (HotpotQA/2Wiki/MuSiQue)
Sec 4.8 ablation: removing register-init-from-seed-evidence or removing iterative updates each independently lowers accuracy, isolating which mechanism components contribute
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Matched-baseline causal design (same generator/tools/corpus), replication across 2 embedding models and 3 standard benchmarks, and a component-level ablation together support the central claim; the generation model itself is only tested as GPT-4o-mini.
reproducibilityEvidence: Full dataset, metric, and hyperparameter details given in the method/experiment sections and appendices; no explicit public code repository link found in the recovered text (a 'this https URL' placeholder appears in the HTML extraction for a related sentence but the underlying code URL could not be confirmed in the sections read)
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: The article states only what the matched-baseline comparison supports (search guidance recovers reachable evidence; it does not by itself verify that evidence correctly), and explicitly reports the side effects (more reasoning errors, more abstentions) rather than presenting the result as a clean win.
candidates.primaryLimitation: Generation model is GPT-4o-mini only; the register is not itself a reliable evidence verifier and can still resolve an item prematurely, and four-hop questions (the hardest case) remain dominated by missing-evidence failures even after the intervention.
candidates.presentationReason: Explicit research-question structure (RQ1-RQ6), a fixed failure-cause taxonomy with a stated priority order for resolving overlaps, and quantified ablations throughout.
candidates.reason: Only candidate today offering a matched-baseline causal decomposition of RAG failure (search-guidance vs evidence-verification bottlenecks) with an accepted oral venue and cross-embedding replication, directly actionable for teams debugging multi-hop RAG/agentic-search pipelines; chosen over 2610.21731's similar-themed but qualitative-only finding and lack of an accepted venue.
